blocks.text: Two days after neck surgery, a 38-year-old woman feels tingling around her mouth and fingertips, and her hand curls into a spasm when a blood pressure cuff is inflated on her arm. Her plasma calcium has fallen by a fraction of a millimole, yet her nerves are firing spontaneously. Calcium is among the most tightly controlled ions in the body, and this unit shows who controls it and what happens when control is lost.

blocks.markdown:
**Why calcium is defended so tightly.** About 99% of body calcium (roughly 1 kg) is in bone as hydroxyapatite, a crystalline calcium phosphate salt. The small plasma pool is vital for nerve and muscle excitability, muscle contraction, hormone secretion, coagulation and intracellular signalling.

Total plasma calcium is about 2.2-2.6 mmol/L (laboratory ranges vary). It exists in three forms: about **50% free ionised Ca2+** (the physiologically active fraction, roughly 1.1-1.3 mmol/L), about **40% bound to albumin**, and about 10% complexed with anions such as citrate and phosphate. Because albumin binding changes with albumin level and with pH, total calcium can mislead; ionised calcium is the quantity regulated. Plasma phosphate is about 0.8-1.5 mmol/L; it is handled separately by the kidney but is linked to calcium through the same hormones and through bone mineral.

blocks.title: Corrected calcium
blocks.text: Corrected (albumin-adjusted) calcium estimates what the total calcium would be if albumin were normal. A commonly used formula is corrected Ca (mmol/L) = measured total Ca + 0.02 x (40 - albumin in g/L). It is an approximation; measured ionised calcium is more reliable when available.

blocks.caption: Calcium in mmol/L, albumin in g/L; 40 g/L is the reference albumin used in this formula.

blocks.markdown:
**Parathyroid hormone (PTH).** PTH is an 84-amino-acid peptide made by the **chief cells** of the four parathyroid glands. A calcium-sensing receptor (a G-protein-coupled receptor) on chief cells detects ionised Ca2+: a fall increases PTH release within minutes, a rise suppresses it. PTH raises plasma calcium by three routes:

- **Bone:** PTH acts on osteoblasts, which signal osteoclasts (via RANKL) to resorb bone, releasing calcium and phosphate.
- **Kidney:** it increases calcium reabsorption in the distal tubule, **decreases phosphate reabsorption** in the proximal tubule (phosphaturia), and stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase to make active vitamin D.
- **Gut (indirect):** via active vitamin D, it increases calcium and phosphate absorption.

The net effect is **raised plasma calcium and lowered plasma phosphate**, which avoids precipitating calcium phosphate in tissues.

blocks.title: Correcting a calcium for low albumin
blocks.prompt: A patient with nephrotic syndrome has total calcium 2.05 mmol/L and albumin 28 g/L. Is the patient truly hypocalcaemic?

steps.text: Find the albumin deficit relative to 40 g/L.
Apply the correction factor of 0.02 mmol/L per g/L.
Compare with the reference range of about 2.2-2.6 mmol/L: the corrected value is normal, so the low reading mostly reflects less albumin-bound calcium, not low ionised calcium.

blocks.answer: Corrected calcium is 2.29 mmol/L, within the usual reference range, so the patient is not truly hypocalcaemic.

blocks.markdown:
**Vitamin D.** Vitamin D is made in or ingested through a two-organ, three-step pathway:

1. **Skin:** ultraviolet B converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3); diet supplies some D2 and D3.
2. **Liver:** 25-hydroxylase converts it to **25-hydroxyvitamin D** (calcidiol), the main circulating and storage form measured in blood.
3. **Kidney (proximal tubule):** 1-alpha-hydroxylase converts it to **1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D** (calcitriol), the active hormone. This step is stimulated by PTH and by low phosphate, and calcitriol itself feeds back to inhibit PTH.

Calcitriol acts through a nuclear receptor to increase **intestinal absorption** of calcium (via calbindin) and phosphate, supports bone mineralisation and acts with PTH on bone resorption. **Calcitonin**, from the parafollicular C cells of the thyroid, lowers plasma calcium by inhibiting osteoclasts; it has only a minor role in adult humans.

blocks.caption: Actions of the main calcium-regulating hormones.
rows: Retains Ca, excretes phosphate, activates vitamin D

blocks.markdown:
**Hypocalcaemia and neuromuscular signs.** Extracellular Ca2+ stabilises the membrane of excitable cells by screening negative surface charges near voltage-gated sodium channels. When ionised Ca2+ falls, the voltage threshold for firing shifts, so nerves discharge spontaneously and repetitively. This causes **perioral and fingertip paraesthesia**, muscle cramps, **carpopedal spasm** and tetany, and in severe cases laryngospasm and seizures. Two classic signs are **Chvostek sign** (tapping the facial nerve in front of the ear twitches the facial muscles) and **Trousseau sign** (inflating a cuff above systolic pressure for about 3 minutes induces carpal spasm). The ECG may show a prolonged QT interval.

Causes include hypoparathyroidism (for example after neck surgery), vitamin D deficiency, and chronic kidney disease (reduced 1-alpha-hydroxylation and phosphate retention). **Alkalosis**, for example from hyperventilation, makes albumin release H+ and bind more Ca2+, so ionised calcium falls even though total calcium is unchanged.

blocks.title: Predicting the effect of parathyroid gland removal
blocks.prompt: After removal of all parathyroid tissue, predict the changes in plasma calcium, plasma phosphate, urinary phosphate excretion and 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D.

steps.text: Without PTH, bone resorption falls and the kidney retains less calcium, so plasma Ca2+ falls (hypocalcaemia).
Without PTH, the proximal tubule reabsorbs more phosphate (less phosphaturia), so plasma phosphate rises (hyperphosphataemia) and urinary phosphate excretion falls.
Without PTH stimulation, 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity falls, so calcitriol falls, reducing gut calcium absorption and compounding the hypocalcaemia.

blocks.answer: Plasma calcium falls, plasma phosphate rises, urinary phosphate excretion falls and calcitriol falls; the low ionised calcium produces neuromuscular excitability and tetany.

items: Ionised calcium falls; the parathyroid calcium-sensing receptor detects it.
PTH mobilises calcium from bone, retains calcium and wastes phosphate in the kidney.
Calcitriol increases gut absorption of calcium and phosphate.
Rising ionised calcium suppresses further PTH release (negative feedback).

blocks.title: PTH and phosphate move in opposite directions
blocks.text: PTH raises calcium and lowers phosphate by increasing phosphate excretion. Hypoparathyroidism therefore gives low calcium and high phosphate; primary hyperparathyroidism gives high calcium and low phosphate. In chronic kidney disease, phosphate retention and low calcitriol give low calcium, high phosphate and high PTH (secondary hyperparathyroidism).

blocks.title: Total calcium is not the regulated quantity
blocks.text: Do not diagnose hypocalcaemia from total calcium alone when albumin is abnormal. Ionised calcium is what the calcium-sensing receptor and excitable membranes respond to, and it also changes with pH independently of total calcium.

points: Ionised plasma calcium is tightly regulated by PTH, calcitriol and, minimally, calcitonin; PTH from chief cells is released when the calcium-sensing receptor detects a fall.
PTH raises calcium by increasing bone resorption and renal calcium reabsorption, while lowering plasma phosphate through phosphaturia and stimulating calcitriol production.
Vitamin D is made in the skin, hydroxylated at position 25 in the liver and at position 1-alpha in the kidney; calcitriol increases intestinal calcium and phosphate absorption.
Hypocalcaemia lowers the threshold for neuronal firing, causing paraesthesia, tetany, Chvostek and Trousseau signs; alkalosis can reduce ionised calcium without changing total calcium.

questions.stem: Which cells secrete parathyroid hormone, and what stimulates its release?

options.text: Chief cells, stimulated by a fall in ionised plasma calcium
Parafollicular C cells, stimulated by a rise in plasma calcium
Chief cells, stimulated by a rise in ionised plasma calcium
Oxyphil cells of the thyroid, stimulated by low plasma phosphate

questions.correctOptionText: Chief cells, stimulated by a fall in ionised plasma calcium

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the calcium-sensing receptor on chief cells detects low Ca2+.
distractorRationale.b: C cells secrete calcitonin, not PTH.
distractorRationale.c: A rise in calcium suppresses PTH secretion.
distractorRationale.d: The parathyroid, not the thyroid, makes PTH, and low phosphate is not the main stimulus.

questions.explanation: Parathyroid chief cells express a calcium-sensing receptor, and a fall in ionised Ca2+ reduces its signalling so PTH is released. This is a negative feedback loop that restores calcium.

questions.stem: Which organ performs the final hydroxylation that produces active 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol)?

distractorRationale.a: Correct: renal 1-alpha-hydroxylase makes calcitriol, stimulated by PTH.
distractorRationale.b: The liver adds the 25-hydroxyl group, giving the storage form.
distractorRationale.c: The skin makes cholecalciferol under ultraviolet B.
distractorRationale.d: The intestine is a target of calcitriol, not its site of synthesis.

questions.explanation: The skin supplies cholecalciferol, the liver converts it to 25-hydroxyvitamin D, and the kidney's 1-alpha-hydroxylase produces the active 1,25-dihydroxy form. Chronic kidney disease therefore impairs activation.

questions.stem: A 16-year-old girl has recurrent muscle cramps and a first seizure. Tapping her facial nerve in front of the ear twitches the facial muscles, and her ECG shows a prolonged QT interval. Investigations suggest autoimmune destruction of the parathyroid glands. Which set of results would be expected?

options.text: Low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH
High calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Low calcium, low phosphate, high PTH
Normal calcium, high phosphate, normal PTH

questions.correctOptionText: Low calcium, high phosphate, low PTH

distractorRationale.a: Correct: absent PTH means less bone and renal calcium mobilisation and more phosphate retention.
distractorRationale.c: Low calcium with high PTH occurs in vitamin D deficiency, but phosphate is not typically low here and PTH is absent after parathyroid injury.
distractorRationale.d: Neuromuscular signs reflect low ionised calcium, so calcium would not be normal.

questions.explanation: A positive Chvostek sign and prolonged QT indicate hypocalcaemia, and parathyroid destruction removes PTH. Without PTH, calcium falls and the kidney reabsorbs more phosphate, giving high plasma phosphate.

questions.stem: A 55-year-old man with advanced chronic kidney disease has low plasma calcium, high plasma phosphate and high PTH. Which mechanism best explains the low calcium?

options.text: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation lowers calcitriol and gut calcium absorption
Excess calcitonin secretion from the thyroid

questions.correctOptionText: Reduced renal 1-alpha-hydroxylation lowers calcitriol and gut calcium absorption

distractorRationale.a: Correct: failing kidneys make less calcitriol and retain phosphate, so calcium falls and PTH rises secondarily.
distractorRationale.b: Calcitonin has a minor role and is not the cause.
distractorRationale.c: 25-hydroxylation is hepatic and is not primarily impaired in CKD.
distractorRationale.d: Primary PTH excess raises calcium rather than lowering it.

questions.explanation: Diseased kidneys lose 1-alpha-hydroxylase activity, so calcitriol falls, intestinal calcium absorption declines and phosphate excretion is impaired. The resulting hypocalcaemia drives secondary hyperparathyroidism.

questions.stem: Parathyroid hormone increases phosphate reabsorption in the proximal tubule of the kidney.
questions.explanation: PTH inhibits proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption, increasing phosphate excretion in urine. This lowers plasma phosphate while PTH raises plasma calcium, preventing calcium phosphate from precipitating.

questions.stem: A patient has measured total calcium 1.95 mmol/L and serum albumin 22 g/L. Using corrected Ca = measured Ca + 0.02 x (40 - albumin in g/L), calculate the corrected calcium in mmol/L.
questions.explanation: The albumin deficit is 40 - 22 = 18 g/L, so the correction is 0.02 x 18 = 0.36 mmol/L. Corrected calcium is 1.95 + 0.36 = 2.31 mmol/L, which is within the usual range, so the low measured value is largely due to low albumin.

questions.stem: The filtered load of calcium is 250 mmol/day. In health 98% is reabsorbed. In untreated hypoparathyroidism the reabsorbed fraction falls to 96%. By how many mmol/day does urinary calcium excretion increase?
questions.explanation: Healthy excretion is 2% of 250 = 5 mmol/day, while with 96% reabsorption it is 4% of 250 = 10 mmol/day. The increase is 5 mmol/day, a doubling, which shows how small changes in reabsorbed fraction matter because PTH normally promotes distal tubular calcium reabsorption.

questions.stem: Describe how parathyroid hormone raises plasma ionised calcium, naming the target organs and the effect on plasma phosphate.
markingGuide: PTH is released by chief cells when the calcium-sensing receptor detects low ionised calcium
Bone: stimulates osteoblasts to signal osteoclasts (RANKL), increasing resorption and releasing calcium and phosphate
Kidney: increases distal tubular calcium reabsorption
Kidney: decreases proximal tubular phosphate reabsorption (phosphaturia), lowering plasma phosphate
Kidney: stimulates 1-alpha-hydroxylase, raising calcitriol, which increases gut calcium and phosphate absorption
Rising calcium inhibits further PTH release (negative feedback)
questions.explanation: PTH works on three target systems at once, and its phosphate-wasting action is what allows plasma calcium to rise without calcium phosphate precipitating in tissues.

questions.stem: Outline the synthesis of active vitamin D, naming each organ, the intermediate formed and the enzyme or stimulus involved, and say how its production is regulated.
markingGuide: Skin: ultraviolet B converts 7-dehydrocholesterol to cholecalciferol (vitamin D3); some vitamin D comes from diet
Liver: 25-hydroxylase forms 25-hydroxyvitamin D (calcidiol), the main storage and circulating form
Kidney (proximal tubule): 1-alpha-hydroxylase forms 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), the active hormone
1-alpha-hydroxylase is stimulated by PTH and low phosphate
Calcitriol inhibits PTH secretion, providing negative feedback
questions.explanation: Active vitamin D is a hormone made by sequential steps in different organs. The tightly regulated renal step lets calcium and phosphate status control calcitriol production.

questions.stem: A 24-year-old student feels tingling in her lips and hands and has carpal spasm during an episode of panic with rapid breathing. Her total calcium is later found to be normal. Explain how hypocalcaemia produces neuromuscular excitability, and how hyperventilation could cause this picture despite a normal total calcium.
markingGuide: Ionised Ca2+ screens surface charge and stabilises voltage-gated sodium channels in nerve and muscle membranes
Low ionised Ca2+ lowers the threshold for firing, so nerves discharge spontaneously: paraesthesia, cramps, carpopedal spasm and tetany
Chvostek and Trousseau signs are clinical signs of this excitability
Hyperventilation blows off CO2 causing respiratory alkalosis
Alkalosis makes albumin release H+ and bind more Ca2+, lowering ionised calcium without changing total calcium
Therefore ionised calcium, not total calcium, determines the signs
questions.explanation: Excitability depends on ionised calcium. Alkalosis shifts calcium onto albumin, so the active fraction falls even when the total looks normal.
